knowledge_point.title: Computing One Iteration of the Newton-Raphson Method

question.:question/problem:
Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[0,2]\times [0,2]⊆{R}^{2},$ where $$ f(x,y)={x}^{2}y-2x-{y}^{2}+1. $$ Calculate one iteration of the Newton-Raphson process for optimization that starts at ${x}_{0}=[1,\,1]^{T}.$ Round your final answer to three decimal places (if needed).
${x}_{1}=$
$1.25$
{{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y-2x-{y}^{2}+1) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y-2x-{y}^{2}+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2xy-2 \\ {x}^{2}-2y\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy-2) & \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-2y) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy-2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-2y)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2y & 2x \\ 2x & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}2y & 2x \\ 2x & -2\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}2xy-2 \\ {x}^{2}-2y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with
${x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{\begin{bmatrix}2y & 2x \\ 2x & -2\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}2xy-2 \\ {x}^{2}-2y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}2(1) & 2(1) \\ 2(1) & -2\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}2(1)(1)-2 \\ (1)^{2}-2(1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{2\cdot (-2)-2\cdot 2}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{8}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1.25 \\ 0.75\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{n}$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{J}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}f({x}_{n}),
$$

where ${J}_{f}({x}_{n})$ is the Jacobian of $f$ evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{3}-6) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{3}-6) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}-3xy+4) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}-3xy+4)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2x & 3{y}^{2} \\ 3{x}^{2}-3y & -3x\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}2x & 3{y}^{2} \\ 3{x}^{2}-3y & -3x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}+{y}^{3}-6 \\ {x}^{3}-3xy+4\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with ${x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{\begin{bmatrix}2x & 3{y}^{2} \\ 3{x}^{2}-3y & -3x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}+{y}^{3}-6 \\ {x}^{3}-3xy+4\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}2(1) & 3(2)^{2} \\ 3(1)^{2}-3(2) & -3(1)\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}(1)^{2}+(2)^{3}-6 \\ (1)^{3}-3(1)(2)+4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}2 & 12 \\ -3 & -3\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{2\cdot (-3)-12\cdot (-3)}\begin{bmatrix}-3 & -12 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{30}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 7\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{9}{10} \\ \frac{53}{30}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}0.9 \\ 1.767\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{n}$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{J}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}f({x}_{n}),
$$

where ${J}_{f}({x}_{n})$ is the Jacobian of $f$ evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}y-x-1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}y-x-1) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}-2y+2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}-2y+2)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3{x}^{2}y-1 & {x}^{3} \\ {y}^{2} & 2xy-2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}3{x}^{2}y-1 & {x}^{3} \\ {y}^{2} & 2xy-2\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{3}y-x-1 \\ x{y}^{2}-2y+2\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

For the second iteration, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}-{\begin{bmatrix}3{x}^{2}y-1 & {x}^{3} \\ {y}^{2} & 2xy-2\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{3}y-x-1 \\ x{y}^{2}-2y+2\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}3(0)^{2}(4)-1 & (0)^{3} \\ (4)^{2} & 2(0)(4)-2\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}(0)^{3}(4)-0-1 \\ (0)(4)^{2}-2(4)+2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 16 & -2\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{(-1)\cdot (-2)-0\cdot 16}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 0 \\ -16 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 22\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 11\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -7\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$1.014$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}y-2x{y}^{2}-x+3{y}^{2}+3) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}y-2x{y}^{2}-x+3{y}^{2}+3)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6xy-2{y}^{2}-1 \\ 3{x}^{2}-4xy+6y\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(6xy-2{y}^{2}-1) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}-4xy+6y) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(6xy-2{y}^{2}-1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}-4xy+6y)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6y & 6x-4y \\ 6x-4y & 6-4x\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}6y & 6x-4y \\ 6x-4y & 6-4x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}6xy-2{y}^{2}-1 \\ 3{x}^{2}-4xy+6y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with
${x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{\begin{bmatrix}6y & 6x-4y \\ 6x-4y & 6-4x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}6xy-2{y}^{2}-1 \\ 3{x}^{2}-4xy+6y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}6(0) & 6(2)-4(0) \\ 6(2)-4(0) & 6-4(2)\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}6(2)(0)-2(0)^{2}-1 \\ 3(2)^{2}-4(2)(0)+6(0)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}0 & 12 \\ 12 & -2\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 12\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{0\cdot (-2)-12\cdot 12}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -12 \\ -12 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 12\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{144}\begin{bmatrix}-142 \\ 12\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}1.014 \\ 0.083\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(-4{x}^{2}y+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2x-3y) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(-4{x}^{2}y+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2x-3y)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-8xy+2x+2 \\ -4{x}^{2}+2y-3\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(-8xy+2x+2) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(-4{x}^{2}+2y-3) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(-8xy+2x+2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(-4{x}^{2}+2y-3)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-8y+2 & -8x \\ -8x & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}-8y+2 & -8x \\ -8x & 2\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}-8xy+2x+2 \\ -4{x}^{2}+2y-3\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

For the second iteration, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}-{\begin{bmatrix}-8y+2 & -8x \\ -8x & 2\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}-8xy+2x+2 \\ -4{x}^{2}+2y-3\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0.2 \\ 0.3\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}-8(0.3)+2 & -8(0.2) \\ -8(0.2) & 2\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}-8(0.2)(0.3)+2(0.2)+2 \\ -4(0.2)^{2}+2(0.3)-3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0.2 \\ 0.3\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}-0.4 & -1.6 \\ -1.6 & 2\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}1.92 \\ -2.56\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0.2 \\ 0.3\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{(-0.4)\cdot 2-(-1.6)\cdot (-1.6)}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1.6 \\ 1.6 & -0.4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1.92 \\ -2.56\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0.2 \\ 0.3\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{3.36}\begin{bmatrix}-0.256 \\ 4.096\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}0.124 \\ 1.519\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[0,2]\times [-1,3]⊆{R}^{2},$ where $$ f(x,y)={x}^{3}-xy-{y}^{2}+3. $$ Calculate the second iteration of the Newton-Raphson process for optimization that starts at ${x}_{0}=[2,\,3]^{T}$ if the first iteration of the algorithm gives ${x}_{1}=[0.96,\,-0.48]^{T}.$ Round your final answer to three decimal places (if needed).
${x}_{2}≈$
{{field-1}}
$-0.221$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}-xy-{y}^{2}+3) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}-xy-{y}^{2}+3)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3{x}^{2}-y \\ -x-2y\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}-y) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(-x-2y) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}-y) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(-x-2y)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6x & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}6x & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}3{x}^{2}-y \\ -x-2y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

For the second iteration, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}-{\begin{bmatrix}6x & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}3{x}^{2}-y \\ -x-2y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0.96 \\ -0.48\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}6(0.96) & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}3(0.96)^{2}-(-0.48) \\ -0.96-2(-0.48)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0.96 \\ -0.48\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}5.76 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}3.2448 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0.96 \\ -0.48\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{5.76\cdot (-2)-(-1)\cdot (-1)}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & 5.76\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3.2448 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0.96 \\ -0.48\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{12.52}\begin{bmatrix}-6.4896 \\ 3.2448\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}0.442 \\ -0.221\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Linear Approximations Near Equilibria

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &={x}^{2}(t)+2y(t)-6 \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=x(t)-3y(t)+{y}^{2}(t)\end{aligned}\right. $$ Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the corresponding linearized system at the equilibrium point ${x}^{∗}=[2,\text{ }1]^{T}?$
${u}^{′}=\,\,$
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}
{{field-3}}{{field-4}}
$\,\,u,\,$
where $u=x-{x}^{∗}$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\boldsymbol{f}(x)
$$

where $x=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and 
$$
\displaystyle \boldsymbol{f}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}+2y-6 \\ x-3y+{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\boldsymbol{f}(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\boldsymbol{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2y-6)=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2y-6)=2 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x-3y+{y}^{2})=1,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x-3y+{y}^{2})=-3+2y\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\boldsymbol{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}2x & 2 \\ 1 & 2y-3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
\boldsymbol{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}2(2) & 2 \\ 1 & 2(1)-3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by

$$
{u}^{′}=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}u,
$$

where the deviation vector is

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x-2 \\ y-1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\boldsymbol{f}(x)
$$

where $x=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and $\boldsymbol{f}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}{y}^{2}-7x \\ {x}^{2}+6y\end{bmatrix}.$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\boldsymbol{f}(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\boldsymbol{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-7x)=-7,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-7x)=2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+6y)=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+6y)=6\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\boldsymbol{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}-7 & 2y \\ 2x & 6\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
\boldsymbol{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}-7 & 2(0) \\ 2(0) & 6\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-7 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by

$$
{u}^{′}=\begin{bmatrix}-7 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{bmatrix}u,
$$

where the deviation vector is

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\boldsymbol{f}(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$

knowledge_point.title: Computing One Iteration of the Newton-Raphson Method

question.:question/problem:
Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[-2,2]\times [0,2]⊆{R}^{2},$ where $$ f(x,y)=2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-xy-2x. $$ Calculate one iteration of the Newton-Raphson process for optimization that starts at ${x}_{0}=[-1,\,0]^{T}.$ Round your final answer to three decimal places (if needed).
${x}_{1}≈$
$0.348$
{{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-xy-2x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-xy-2x)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4x{y}^{2}+6x-y-2 \\ 4{x}^{2}y-x\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x{y}^{2}+6x-y-2) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(4{x}^{2}y-x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(4x{y}^{2}+6x-y-2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{2}y-x)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4{y}^{2}+6 & 8xy-1 \\ 8xy-1 & 4{x}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}4{y}^{2}+6 & 8xy-1 \\ 8xy-1 & 4{x}^{2}\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}4x{y}^{2}+6x-y-2 \\ 4{x}^{2}y-x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with
${x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{\begin{bmatrix}4{y}^{2}+6 & 8xy-1 \\ 8xy-1 & 4{x}^{2}\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}4x{y}^{2}+6x-y-2 \\ 4{x}^{2}y-x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}4(0)^{2}+6 & 8(-1)(0)-1 \\ 8(-1)(0)-1 & 4(-1)^{2}\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}4(-1)(0)^{2}+6(-1)-0-2 \\ 4(-1)^{2}(0)-(-1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}6 & -1 \\ -1 & 4\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}-8 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{6\cdot 4-(-1)\cdot (-1)}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-8 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{23}\begin{bmatrix}-31 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}0.348 \\ 0.087\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(4{x}^{2}y-2{x}^{2}+xy-3{y}^{2}-2) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{2}y-2{x}^{2}+xy-3{y}^{2}-2)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8xy-4x+y \\ 4{x}^{2}+x-6y\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(8xy-4x+y) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(4{x}^{2}+x-6y) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(8xy-4x+y) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{2}+x-6y)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8y-4 & 8x+1 \\ 8x+1 & -6\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$

$$

Starting with
${x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{\begin{bmatrix}8y-4 & 8x+1 \\ 8x+1 & -6\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}8xy-4x+y \\ 4{x}^{2}+x-6y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}8(2)-4 & 8(1)+1 \\ 8(1)+1 & -6\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}8(1)(2)-4(1)+2 \\ 4(1)^{2}+(1)-6(2)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}12 & 9 \\ 9 & -6\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}14 \\ -7\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{12\cdot (-6)-9\cdot 9}\begin{bmatrix}-6 & -9 \\ -9 & 12\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}14 \\ -7\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{153}\begin{bmatrix}-21 \\ -210\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}0.863 \\ 0.627\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
